tldr: Across 16 country buckets, headlines split between two dominant axes: roughly half lead with the arson arrest, treating crime as the primary news peg, while the other half foreground mass displacement and structural destruction. France Info and Le Devoir stand apart with a personal evacuee voice and a war-zone metaphor respectively; India is alone in naming a celebrity and questioning government preparedness.

single_outlet_findings.finding: Only outlet to foreground the suspect's criminal history in the headline itself — 'Convicted felon arrested' — subordinating the disaster to the accused's character rather than scale or cause.
Leads with a direct personal quotation ('Il est temps pour moi de partir') as the headline — the only outlet to put an evacuee voice at the front rather than a statistic or the arrest.

The only outlet to embed both a celebrity name (Spencer Pratt) and an anti-government sentiment ('Don't expect govt to…') in its headline — tabloid-adjacent framing absent from every other bucket in the corpus.

Invokes a war-zone metaphor ('comparables à une zone de guerre') as the headline frame — the only outlet to elevate the disaster to humanitarian-crisis register in its headline rather than lead with statistics or the arrest.

Headlines with 'Major Pacific Northwest City Devastated By Massive Wildfires' — the only major US outlet to lead solely with disaster scale and geography, omitting any reference to arson or the arrest.

bottom_line: Headline coverage frames the Spokane wildfires as a crime story first — arson arrest leading in wire services and most Anglophone outlets — layered over a mass-displacement disaster, with structural causes (drought, firefighting capacity) visible only in Al Jazeera's and The Independent's explanatory headlines, and India uniquely injecting celebrity and government-failure angles absent everywhere else.
